Grass-Land Region - Pampas - Argentina.
The Pampas is the temperate grassland of South America and lies mainly in Argentina, where commercial cattle rearing is practised on it.

Toys - Paper Industry - Small-Scale Industry.
Toy making and paper making both need limited capital and a small workforce, so both are classified as small-scale industries.

Population Explosion - Bangladesh - Niger.
Both countries have a high birth rate with a falling death rate, which is the condition that produces a population explosion.

(D) Trade.
Tertiary activities neither take anything directly from nature nor manufacture goods; they provide services and carry out exchange. Fishing and animal husbandry are primary activities and the sugar industry is secondary.

(C) Transportation.
Climate, soils and relief are physical factors. Transportation is created by people, so it is a human factor affecting where population settles.

(B) Wheat.
Extensive commercial grain farming is practised on very large temperate farms with machinery, and its main crop is wheat. Coffee is a plantation crop and rice is grown by intensive subsistence farming.

(A) Pune Metropolitan.
A functional region is organised around a node and is bounded by the reach of that node's activity. Latur, Satara and Amravati are administrative districts, which are formal regions.

(C) Public Sector.
Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited is owned and run by the Government of India, so it belongs to the public sector.

Descending order of capital investment:
(c) Large scale industry - (d) Medium scale industry - (a) Small scale industry - (b) Micro scale industry.

(c) Hunting.
Research, training and teaching are quaternary activities based on knowledge. Hunting is a primary activity, so it is the incorrect factor.

West to East:
(d) U.S.A. - (a) France - (b) India - (c) Japan.
The U.S.A. lies west of the Prime Meridian; France is just east of it; India is further east and Japan furthest east of the four.

(d) China.
In the late expanding stage the birth rate falls quickly while the death rate is already low, so growth slows but continues. Germany and Sweden are in the low stationary or declining stage and Congo is still early expanding.

(b) shallow seas, confluence of warm and cold ocean currents, growth of planktons, cold climate.
Shallow seas let sunlight reach the sea bed, the meeting of warm and cold currents brings up nutrients, planktons then multiply and feed the fish, and a cold climate helps preserve the catch.

False.
Population changes through three components - births, deaths and migration. Migration redistributes people between places and is therefore a component of population change.

True.
The transitional belt where a city gradually gives way to the countryside, and where both urban and rural land uses are found together, is called the rural-urban fringe.

True.
Relief, soil, water and climate are physical factors and capital, technology, transport and government policy are human factors, and agriculture develops where these come together favourably.

False.
The factors differ from place to place. An industry may be pulled by raw material in one region, by cheap power in another and by the market in a third, so no single set of factors applies everywhere.

Ratnagiri and Sindhudurg grow large quantities of mango, cashew and kokum. Fruit is bulky and perishable, so it spoils and loses weight if carried far. Processing it close to the orchards keeps the fruit fresh, cuts transport cost and gives local people work, so fruit processing industries are located there.

The Himalayan region has steep slopes, thin stony soil and very cold winters with heavy snow. Farming is difficult, building is costly and transport links are few, so it cannot support many people and the population remains low.

Relief, climate, soil, water and minerals decide what activities are possible in a region. A level, well watered and mineral rich region can support agriculture, industry and transport and so develops quickly, while a rugged, dry or barren region cannot. Hence regional development depends on the physical setting.

A literate population can use new methods, take up skilled work and earn more, and it also looks after health and family size better. Literacy therefore rises and falls with the social and economic condition of a country, which makes it a reliable indicator of development.

A rural settlement becomes urban only when non-agricultural work, transport links and services grow there. Villages far from roads and markets, or where farming remains the only occupation, do not attract such growth, so they continue as rural settlements.

No region produces everything it needs, because relief, climate, soil and minerals differ from place to place. A region sells what it has in surplus and buys what it lacks, and this difference between regions is what makes trade necessary.

Donor region: the region people move OUT of. Its population falls, the working age group and often the men leave, its sex ratio and age structure become unbalanced, and labour becomes short.
Recipient region: the region people move IN to. Its population rises, it gains workers in the working age group, but pressure grows on housing, water and services and slums may develop.

Shifting Agriculture: subsistence farming of tropical forests; a patch is cleared and burnt, cropped for two or three years, then abandoned; small plots, simple tools, low yield.
Plantation Agriculture: commercial farming of a single cash crop such as tea, coffee or rubber; very large estates, heavy capital, hired labour, scientific methods and high output meant for export.

Waterways: the cheapest means for heavy and bulky goods; very slow; needs no track to be built, only ports; limited to coasts, rivers and canals.
Airways: the fastest means and the costliest; carries light, valuable or urgent goods and passengers; needs airports and skilled staff; can cross mountains, deserts and oceans that other means cannot.

Physical Geography: studies the natural environment - relief, climate, soils, water, plants and animals. Its branches include geomorphology, climatology and oceanography.
Human Geography: studies people and their activities - population, settlements, economic activities and culture. Its branches include population geography, settlement geography and economic geography.

Formal region: uniform throughout in one or more chosen features, such as a wheat growing region or a language region; it has distinct boundaries and does not change quickly.
Functional region: organised around a node such as a city, port or station; it is not uniform inside, its boundary is where the node's influence ends, and it changes as that influence grows or shrinks.

People migrate for push and pull reasons.
Push factors drive people out: poverty, unemployment, small and fragmented holdings, drought, flood, earthquake, war and social or political persecution.
Pull factors draw people in: jobs, higher wages, education, medical and other services, security and a better standard of living.
Migration may also be forced, as when people are displaced by a dam or a war, and it is these reasons together that decide its direction and volume.

Regional imbalance means some regions of India develop much faster than others.
Its causes are: an unfavourable physical setting such as rugged relief, drought or poor soil; poor transport and power supply; lack of minerals or industry; low literacy and poor health services; concentration of investment in a few already developed regions; and historical neglect of some areas.
The result is that people, industry and income concentrate in a few regions while others remain backward, which is why balanced regional development is a stated aim of planning.

Birth rate and death rate together decide natural growth.
When both are high, growth is very slow, because the many births are cancelled by the many deaths.
When the death rate falls while the birth rate stays high, the gap between the two widens and population grows very fast. This is the stage of population explosion.
When the birth rate also falls, the gap narrows again and growth slows.
When both are low, growth is nearly nil and the population becomes stable or may even decline.

Communication means carrying information, not goods or people.
Personal means carry a message to one named person, such as post, telegram, telephone and e-mail.
Mass means carry a message to many people at once, such as newspapers, radio, television and the internet.
Modern communication depends on satellites, optical fibre and mobile networks, which have made contact instant and cheap over any distance and have reduced the need to travel.

Geography studies the earth as the home of people and explains the difference between one place and another.
Its nature is dualistic: it studies the physical environment and human activity together, and it is both a natural science and a social science.
It is spatial, because it always asks where a thing is and why it is there; it is integrating, because it draws on many other subjects; and it is dynamic, because both the earth and human activity keep changing.

They were the main market places and the bases of wealthy merchants, land and livestock owners and traders, and they were educational centres and homes of handicraft industry. In all these roles they were the focal points of power, authority and change.

Extensive commercial grain farming is practised on very large farms for sale, not for the family's own use.
Characteristics: the farm is very large, often several hundred hectares; only one crop is grown, mainly wheat, so it is a monoculture; almost all the work is done by machines such as tractors, seed drills, harvesters and combines; the labour force is very small; yield per hectare is low but total production is very high because of the great area; the whole produce is sold, so the farm depends on the market, on transport and on grain elevators for storage.
Distribution: it is found in the temperate grasslands - the Prairies of Canada and the U.S.A., the Pampas of Argentina, the Steppes of Ukraine and Russia, the Downs of Australia and the Veld of South Africa. These regions have level land, moderate rainfall, fertile soil and a thin population, which is the combination the system needs.

The location of an industry is decided by many factors together, and the factor that weighs most differs from one industry to another.
Physical factors: raw material, because industries that use bulky or perishable raw material such as sugar, cement and fruit processing are set up near the source; power, since industries needing large amounts of energy stay near coal fields or power stations; climate, as the cotton textile industry prefers humid air and the film and electronics industries need dust free conditions; water, needed in large quantity by iron and steel, paper and chemical industries; and level land on which to build.
Economic and human factors: the market, which pulls industries making bulky, fragile or perishable finished goods; transport, since every industry needs to bring in material and send out goods cheaply; labour, both cheap and skilled; capital and banking; and government policy, which through concessions and industrial estates can place an industry where it would not otherwise go.
Footloose industries such as watch and diamond cutting are tied to none of these strongly and can be located almost anywhere.
